title: The largest private funders of City-paid organizations
question: Which grantmakers put the most money into organizations the City also pays, to whom, and how concentrated is each one's giving?
finding: 959 grantmakers paid $2.10 billion to 442 City-paid organizations in tax periods ending 2020 to 2025; the ten largest account for $1.19 billion (57%). The largest: Silicon Valley Community Foundation $243.3 million to 231 organizations; Crankstart Foundation $238.3 million to 126 organizations; The San Francisco Foundation $196.9 million to 289 organizations; East Bay Community Foundation $99.3 million to 112 organizations. $745.2 million came through community foundations and other public-charity grantmakers, and $227.6 million of the total went to one recipient, Tides Center. Among the 60 largest funders, 13 sent more than half of their City-paid-organization giving to a single recipient.
how: Every grant paid, with a named recipient, in the latest version of each funder's return was matched to the organizations the City paid $750,000 or more in fiscal 2019 to 2026 (or $250,000 in fiscal 2026), by federal employer number where the return prints one and otherwise by exact name and address. Dollars were added by funder. 'Largest recipient' and 'five largest' are shares of the funder's giving to City-paid organizations; the next columns set that giving against everything the funder itemised, and show what it paid without naming a recipient. Matching: 17,504 grant rows were taken to be City-paid organizations, 3,430 of them on an employer number and the rest on name and address (639 of those on a one-word name, kept only with a matching address and labelled). Set aside and in no total: 969 rows ($47.1 million) where the same name is printed with an address in another city, 15 one-word names with no matching address, and $1.57 billion to universities, public bodies and organizations the City paid less than $750,000. Rows with a negative or blank amount are left out.
limits: Funding an organization the City also pays is ordinary philanthropy. Community foundations hold donor-advised funds (accounts whose donors recommend the grants), and their returns do not say which grants a donor recommended, so their totals are not one board's choices. Totals across funders are not all new money: a grant to a fiscal sponsor or to another grantmaker is paid out again and can appear a second time. Private-foundation returns carry no recipient number, so those rows are name matches. A funder's rows that name no recipient are in none of the sums.
